theory_refs.why: Why two pointers (which needs sorting) is the wrong tool here.

theory_refs.at: The inner loop searches for one known value

theory_refs.why: Why inserting first pairs an element with itself.
What "O(1)" really means for a hash map.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(unsorted array a, target) → indices [i, j], i ≠ j, with a[i] + a[j] = target. Exactly one answer exists.
- n ≤ 10⁴ (so O(n²) actually passes — but the follow-up asks for better than O(n²), and interviews always do).
- Values up to ±10⁹.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Target complexity: O(n) or O(n log n).
✍️ By hand on [2, 7, 11, 15], target 9: at 2 I think "I need a 7" and my eyes scan for 7. That scan is the expensive part.
✍️ Hard part: finding the partner without scanning, while still returning **original indices** (so sorting is awkward).
✍️ Edges: [3, 3] target 6 (equal values); [3, 2, 4] target 6 (3 must not pair with itself).

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** All pairs i < j. O(n²) time, O(1) space.
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: the inner loop. Its job: "search the array for the value target − a[i]".
✍️ ↳ Unlock: "Am I searching for something I could have remembered?" — yes, a specific known value.
✍️ **2. Better (sort + two pointers).** O(n log n), but sorting loses the original indices; you must sort (value, index) pairs. Workable, more code.
✍️ **3. Better (two-pass hash).** Put every value → index in a map, then look up target − a[i] for each i, making sure the index found is not i. O(n).
✍️ **4. Optimal (one-pass hash).** Look up first, insert after. Only earlier elements are in the map → no self-pairing check needed, and you stop at the first hit. O(n) time, O(n) space.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Create an empty map from value to index.
✍️ 2. Walk the array. For element x at index i, compute need = target − x.
✍️ 3. If need is in the map, return [map[need], i].
✍️ 4. Otherwise store x → i and continue.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   seen = map value → index (empty)
LOOP    for i in 0..n-1, x = a[i]
CHECK     need = target - x
          if need in seen: return [seen[need], i]
UPDATE    seen[x] = i                  ← after the check
RETURN  []                             (unreachable: an answer is guaranteed)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Dry run
stages.body:
Input [3, 2, 4], target 6:
| i | x | need | in seen? | seen after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| start | | | | {} |
| 0 | 3 | 3 | no (3 is not inserted yet) | {3:0} |
| 1 | 2 | 4 | no | {3:0, 2:1} |
| 2 | 4 | 2 | yes → return [1, 2] | |
If we had inserted before checking, i = 0 would have found 3 and returned [0, 0].

stages.title: Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) average time, O(n) space. Brute force is the classic O(n²) time / O(1) space trade-off.
✍️ Duplicates [3, 3]: at i = 1, need 3 is already in the map from i = 0 → [0, 1]. Correct because we check before inserting.
- Overflow check: values and target are within ±10⁹, so `target − a[i]` is within ±2·10⁹ — just inside int's limit of ≈ 2.147·10⁹. Fine here, but in variants with larger values use `long long need` ([[cpp-integer-overflow#ranges]]).

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Pair search on **unsorted** data → store what you have seen, look up what you need.
✍️ Always **check, then insert** when an element must not pair with itself.
✍️ The map's value is whatever the question asks for: index here, count when counting pairs, last index when distance matters.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *The array is sorted; O(1) space?* Two pointers from both ends (tomorrow, [[tp-opposite-ends]]).
- *Return all pairs / count pairs.* Store counts; add count[need] at each step.
- *Three numbers summing to target?* Sort + fix one + two pointers (tomorrow's 3Sum).
- *What if the input does not fit in memory?* Sort externally and two-pointer, or hash-partition the data into chunks by value.

siblings.title: Contains Duplicate
siblings.maps: The complement of x is x itself — so a set (no index needed) answers "seen before?".

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Return true if any value appears at least twice.
✍️ Brute: all pairs O(n²). Sort and compare neighbours: O(n log n), O(1) extra.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ The question at each element is "have I seen this exact value?" → hash set. Check, then insert. O(n) time, O(n) space.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Walk the array; if the value is already in the set, return true; otherwise insert it. Return false at the end.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
seen = empty set
for x in a:
    if x in seen: return true
    seen.insert(x)
return false
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body:
✍️ Set = map without values; use it when you only need membership ([[cpp-unordered-map-set#api]]).
- Trade-off talk: sorting gives O(1) extra space at O(n log n) time.

siblings.title: Number of Good Pairs
siblings.maps: Count pairs instead of finding one: the map stores counts and every earlier equal value forms a pair.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Count pairs i < j with a[i] == a[j].

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Brute O(n²). Complement = x itself; when x arrives, it pairs with every earlier x → add cnt[x], then cnt[x]++.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each x: answer += count of x seen so far; then increment the count.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cnt = map; ans = 0
for x in a: ans += cnt[x]; cnt[x] += 1
return ans
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Counting pairs → map value is a **count**; still query before recording ([[hash-complement-lookup#variations]]).

siblings.title: Contains Duplicate II
siblings.maps: Store the last index of each value; a duplicate counts only if it is within distance k.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ True if some value appears at indices i ≠ j with |i − j| ≤ k.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ For each x, the best earlier partner is its **most recent** occurrence (closest). Map value → last index. O(n). (Window alternative: a set of the last k elements.)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each i: if x was seen and i − last[x] ≤ k → true. Update last[x] = i.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
last = map
for i, x in a:
    if x in last and i - last[x] <= k: return true
    last[x] = i
return false
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ The map value is chosen by what the check needs: here the **latest** index.

theory_refs.at: One table: ++ for s, −− for t

theory_refs.why: Why an array is the right container for lowercase letters.
Different lengths can never be anagrams.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(s, t) → true if t is a rearrangement of s (same letters, same counts).
- Lowercase English letters, length ≤ 5·10⁴.
- "anagram", "nagaram" → true; "rat", "car" → false.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Order does not matter; only how many of each letter. That is a frequency question.
✍️ Hard part: none conceptually — the decision is which container to use.
✍️ Edges: different lengths → false immediately; one character.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** For each character of s, find and remove one copy from t. O(n²).
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: searching t for each character.
✍️ **2. Better.** Sort both strings and compare. O(n log n).
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: sorting establishes a full order, but we only need equal counts.
✍️ **3. Optimal.** Count letters: +1 for s, −1 for t; all 26 must end at 0. O(n) time, O(1) space (26 is a constant).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. If the lengths differ, return false.
✍️ 2. Make an array of 26 zeros.
✍️ 3. For each position, add 1 for s's letter and subtract 1 for t's letter.
✍️ 4. Return true iff every entry is 0.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   if len(s) != len(t): return false
        cnt[26] = 0
LOOP    for i in 0..n-1
UPDATE    cnt[s[i]-'a']++ ; cnt[t[i]-'a']--
CHECK   for k in 0..25: if cnt[k] != 0: return false
RETURN  true
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Dry run
stages.body:
s = "rat", t = "car":
| i | s[i] | t[i] | changed counts |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | r | c | r:+1, c:−1 |
| 1 | a | a | a: 0 |
| 2 | t | r | t:+1, r:0 |
Final non-zeros: c = −1, t = +1 → false.

stages.title: Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space (fixed 26 counters).
- Unicode follow-up: the alphabet is no longer small → `unordered_map<char32_t,int>` or a map over code points.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ "Same multiset of items" → count, don't sort.
✍️ Two inputs to compare → one table with + and −; check all zero.
✍️ Letters only → `int cnt[26]` with `c − 'a'`.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *What if inputs contain Unicode?* Hash map keyed by character.
- *Group many words into anagram groups.* The sorted word (or count signature) becomes a key ([[hash-derived-keys]]).
- *Find all anagrams of p inside s.* Fixed window of counts (Day 8, [[str-anagram-window]]).

siblings.title: Group Anagrams
siblings.maps: Instead of comparing two words, compute each word's canonical key and group words with equal keys.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Group the words that are anagrams of each other; any order.
✍️ Brute: compare every pair with Valid Anagram → O(n² · L).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body:
✍️ Bottleneck: pairwise comparison. Fix: two words are anagrams iff their sorted forms are equal → use the sorted form as a hash-map key → O(n · L log L).
✍️ (Count signature key gives O(n · L).)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each word, sort a copy to get its key; append the word to groups[key]. Output all groups.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
groups = map key → list
for w in words: key = sorted(w); groups[key].append(w)
return all lists in groups
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body:
✍️ "Group items that are equivalent" → canonical key + map of lists ([[hash-derived-keys#idea]]).
✍️ Key choice trade-off: sorted string vs count signature ([[hash-derived-keys#key-choice]]).

siblings.title: Ransom Note
siblings.maps: Count the magazine's letters, then spend them on the note — a count may never go negative.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Can the note be built using each magazine letter at most once?

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Count magazine letters; for each note letter decrement; if any count drops below 0 → false. O(n + m).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Count the supply, consume the demand, fail on a shortage.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cnt[26] from magazine
for c in note: cnt[c]--; if cnt[c] < 0: return false
return true
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Supply/demand counting: the same ++/−− table, with an early exit on a shortage ([[hash-frequency-counting#variations]]).

siblings.title: First Unique Character in a String
siblings.maps: Count in pass 1; pass 2 restores the original order and returns the first count of 1.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Index of the first character that appears exactly once, or −1.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ For each character scan the whole string → O(n²). Two passes with counts → O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Count all letters; walk the string again and return the first index whose letter count is 1.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cnt[26] from s
for i in 0..n-1: if cnt[s[i]] == 1: return i
return -1
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Counting loses order; a second pass over the input gets it back.

theory_refs.why: The three levels and what each costs.
A banned data structure names the technique.
The order of the two lines in the loop.

theory_refs.at: Why the survivor is the majority

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(array) → the value that appears more than ⌊n/2⌋ times (guaranteed to exist).
- n ≤ 5·10⁴. Follow-up: O(n) time and O(1) space.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ First solve it with what you know today (a frequency map). Then the follow-up removes the map — that is the TWIST.
✍️ By hand on [2,2,1,1,1,2,2]: imagine pairing each 1 with a 2 and throwing both away. 2s are left over. The majority always survives this.
✍️ Edges: n = 1; majority at the very end.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** For each value count it with a scan. O(n²).
✍️ **2. Better (frequency map).** Count all, return the one with count > n/2. O(n) time, O(n) space.
✍️ **3. Better (sort).** The majority must cover the middle index → return a[n/2]. O(n log n), O(1).
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck for O(1) space: storing a count for **every** value, when only one value matters.
✍️ ↳ Unlock: "a forbidden data structure is a hint" — no map means a counting/cancelling argument.
✍️ **4. Optimal (Boyer–Moore).** One candidate + one counter; equal → +1, different → −1, counter 0 → adopt the new value. O(n), O(1).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Start with no candidate and count 0.
✍️ 2. For each value: if the count is 0, make this value the candidate.
✍️ 3. If the value equals the candidate, increase the count; otherwise decrease it.
✍️ 4. The candidate at the end is the majority.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   cand = none; cnt = 0
LOOP    for x in a
UPDATE    if cnt == 0: cand = x          (adopt FIRST)
          cnt += (x == cand) ? +1 : -1
RETURN  cand
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) time, O(1) space.
✍️ The result is guaranteed only because a majority is guaranteed. Without the guarantee, verify with a second counting pass.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ Always solve it the "known" way first (frequency map), then remove the expensive part.
✍️ "O(1) extra space" on a counting problem → think cancellation (Boyer–Moore), XOR, or arithmetic — never a smarter map.
✍️ Majority > n/k → at most k−1 candidates.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Elements appearing more than n/3 times* (LeetCode 229): two candidates, two counters, verify at the end.
- *No majority guaranteed?* Second pass to count the candidate.
- *Why does sorting work?* A value covering more than half the positions must cover index n/2.

siblings.title: Majority Element II
siblings.maps: More than n/3 → at most two survivors; keep two candidates and two counters, then verify.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Return all values appearing more than ⌊n/3⌋ times; O(1) space follow-up.
✍️ At most two such values can exist (three would need more than n elements).

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Map → O(n) space. Voting with two candidates: a value different from **both** cancels one copy of each. Survivors are only candidates → count them again to verify.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ 1. Pass 1: if x matches a candidate, increment its count; else if a count is 0, adopt x there; else decrement both. 2. Pass 2: count both candidates; keep those > n/3.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
c1, c2 = none; n1 = n2 = 0
for x in a:
    if x == c1: n1++
    elif x == c2: n2++
    elif n1 == 0: c1 = x; n1 = 1
    elif n2 == 0: c2 = x; n2 = 1
    else: n1--; n2--
verify counts of c1, c2 > n/3
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Check "matches a candidate" **before** "a count is 0", or the same value can occupy both slots ([[hash-boyer-moore-voting#variations]]).

siblings.title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
siblings.maps: Values are 1..n, so the array itself can be the "seen" table — mark index v−1 negative.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Array of n values in [1, n]; return the values in [1, n] that never appear. Follow-up: no extra space.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Set of seen values → O(n) space. In place: for each value v, make a[|v|−1] negative. Indices still positive at the end were never marked.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Mark; then collect i+1 for every positive a[i].

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
for x in a: i = |x| - 1; a[i] = -|a[i]|
for i in 0..n-1: if a[i] > 0: output i+1
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Values in 1..n → index-as-key marking ([[arr-in-place-tricks#index-as-key]]). Use `abs` because earlier marks made some values negative.

siblings.title: Sort Array by Increasing Frequency
siblings.maps: Count frequencies, then sort with a comparator that reads the counts.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Sort by frequency ascending; ties by value descending.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Frequency map, then `sort` with a two-key comparator. O(n log n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Count; sort with (freq ascending, value descending).

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
cnt = frequency map
sort a by (cnt[x] asc, x desc)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ Two-key comparators: compare the first key, fall back to the second; never use `<=` ([[cpp-sort-and-comparators#strict]]).

theory_refs.why: The constraint that rules out sorting.

theory_refs.at: Re-walking each run from every element
theory_refs.why: Why the naive set version is O(n²).

theory_refs.at: Iterate the set, not the array
Why the nested loop is O(n)
theory_refs.why: Charge each value to one walk.

stages.title: Understand
stages.body:
✍️ f(unsorted array) → length of the longest set of values that form consecutive integers v, v+1, …, v+L−1 (positions do not matter).
- n ≤ 10⁵, must be O(n).
- [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2] → 4 (1, 2, 3, 4).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ This is a DISGUISE: nothing says "hash set", but the O(n) requirement on unsorted data does.
✍️ By hand: I look at 4 and ask "is 5 there? is 3 there?". If I always start counting from the smallest number of a run, I count each run once.
✍️ Hard part: avoiding counting the same run many times.
✍️ Edges: empty array → 0; duplicates [1, 2, 0, 1] → 3; negatives.

stages.title: Brainstorm: brute → optimal
stages.body:
✍️ **1. Brute.** For each value v, check v+1, v+2, … by scanning the array each time. O(n³) worst.
✍️ **2. Better.** Sort, then scan counting runs and skipping duplicates. O(n log n) — fails the O(n) requirement.
✍️ **3. Better.** Put values in a set; for each value walk upward with O(1) lookups. O(n²) on input like 1..n (each run walked from every element).
✍️ ↳ Bottleneck: a run of length L is walked L times.
✍️ ↳ Unlock: every run has exactly one start — the value whose predecessor is missing. Walk only from starts.
✍️ **4. Optimal.** Set + start-of-run. Each value is part of exactly one walk → O(n).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body:
✍️ 1. Insert all values into a hash set.
✍️ 2. For each value v in the set: if v − 1 is also in the set, skip it (not a start).
✍️ 3. Otherwise walk v+1, v+2, … while present, counting the length.
✍️ 4. Keep the maximum length.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
STATE   s = set(a); best = 0
LOOP    for v in s                       (the set, so duplicates are gone)
CHECK     if (v - 1) in s: continue      (not the start of a run)
UPDATE    len = 1
          while (v + len) in s: len++
          best = max(best, len)
RETURN  best
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Edge cases and complexity
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) average time: n inserts; each value is checked once as a possible start and visited at most once by a walk. O(n) space.
✍️ Empty input → the loop never runs → 0.
- `v + len` with v near INT_MAX could overflow in theory; LeetCode's range is ±10⁹, so it is safe.

stages.title: Carry forward
stages.body:
✍️ O(n) required + unsorted + "consecutive / sequence" → hash set, not sorting.
✍️ To count each group once, start only from its canonical first member.
✍️ A loop inside a loop can still be O(n) if each element is charged to one inner walk.

stages.title: Interview follow-ups
stages.body:
- *Return the sequence itself.* Remember the start of the best run.
- *Streaming input?* Union-find or a map of run boundaries (value → length of run ending/starting here), updating neighbours on insert.
- *Why not sort?* O(n log n) violates the requirement; mention it as the simpler fallback.

siblings.title: Longest Square Streak in an Array
siblings.maps: "Next element" is v² instead of v+1; same set lookups, walking from each value.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Longest subsequence that, after sorting, has each element equal to the square of the previous; length ≥ 2, else −1.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Put values in a set. From each v, walk v → v² → v⁴ while present. Values ≤ 10⁵ so a chain has at most ~5 steps → O(n · 5). (Start-of-run trick optional here because chains are tiny.)

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ For each value, follow squares through the set counting the chain; track the max; return −1 if < 2.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
s = set(a); best = 0
for v in s:
    len = 0; x = v
    while x in s: len++; x = x*x   (long long, stop if x > 1e5)
    best = max(best, len)
return best >= 2 ? best : -1
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body:
✍️ The "successor" can be any function (v+1, v², 2v); set membership makes each step O(1) ([[hash-set-runs#idea]]).
✍️ Squaring overflows int fast → `long long` and a bound check ([[cpp-integer-overflow#where]]).

siblings.title: Intersection of Two Arrays
siblings.maps: Set membership across two inputs; a second set removes duplicates from the answer.

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body: ✍️ Distinct values present in both arrays.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Set of the first array; for each value of the second that is in the set, output it once (erase it from the set after use).

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Build a set from a; scan b; output and erase on a hit.

stages.title: Pseudocode
stages.body:
```
s = set(a); out = []
for x in b: if x in s: out.append(x); s.erase(x)
```

stages.title: Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body: ✍️ `erase(key)` returns how many were removed — a neat "was it there?" check.

siblings.title: First Missing Positive
siblings.maps: A set solves it in O(n) space; the O(1)-space version places each value v at index v−1 (cyclic placement).

stages.title: Analyse
stages.body:
✍️ Smallest positive integer not in the array; O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
✍️ The answer is in 1..n+1, so only values in [1, n] matter.

stages.title: Brainstorm
stages.body: ✍️ Set of values, then test 1, 2, 3, … → O(n) time, O(n) space. For O(1): swap each value v ∈ [1, n] into position v−1 until positions are stable; then the first i with a[i] ≠ i+1 gives i+1.

stages.title: Algorithm in words
stages.body: ✍️ Cyclic placement, then scan for the first misplaced index.

stages.title: Pseudocode
Reference C++
Quick theory
stages.body:
✍️ Each swap puts one value in its final place → O(n) total ([[arr-in-place-tricks#cyclic]]).
✍️ The guard `a[a[i]−1] != a[i]` stops infinite swapping on duplicates.

drill.title: Check if the Sentence Is Pangram
drill.statement: Decide whether a lowercase sentence uses every letter of the alphabet at least once.
drill.approach: Mark each letter seen in a bool[26] (or set); true iff all 26 marked.
drill.trigger: "every letter / all characters" over a fixed alphabet.

drill.title: Isomorphic Strings
drill.statement: Two strings of equal length; decide whether the characters of the first can be replaced one-to-one to produce the second.
drill.approach: Keep two maps s→t and t→s; at each position both must agree with earlier mappings (or both be new). Equivalent: compare the "first occurrence index" patterns of both strings.
drill.trigger: "one-to-one mapping / same pattern" between two sequences.

drill.title: Word Pattern
drill.statement: Given a pattern like "abba" and a sentence of words, decide whether the words follow the pattern with a one-to-one letter↔word mapping.
drill.approach: Split the sentence; lengths must match; maintain char→word and word→char maps and reject any conflict.
drill.trigger: "follows the same pattern" → bijection check with two hash maps.

drill.title: Unique Number of Occurrences
drill.statement: Return true if no two distinct values in the array occur the same number of times.
drill.pattern_name: Count, then check the counts are distinct
drill.approach: Frequency map; insert every count into a set; true iff the set size equals the number of distinct values.
drill.trigger: question is about the counts themselves → count first, then reason about counts.

drill.title: How Many Numbers Are Smaller Than the Current Number
drill.statement: For each element, report how many other elements are strictly smaller. Values are between 0 and 100.
drill.approach: Values are small → count each value, take a running prefix of counts; answer for x is the total count of values < x.
drill.trigger: small value range (0..100) → counting array instead of sorting or nested loops.

sections.title: Concept
sections.body:
✍️ **Encapsulation** = bundling data with the functions that operate on it, and **hiding** the data so it can only be changed through those functions.
✍️ Why: the class can enforce its own rules (an account balance never goes negative), and the internal representation can change without breaking code that uses the class.
✍️ C++ access specifiers: `private` (only the class itself and friends), `protected` (also derived classes), `public` (everyone).
✍️ Getters/setters expose controlled access; a setter can validate before changing state.

sections.title: C++ example
Interview questions
sections.body:
✍️ **Q: Encapsulation vs abstraction?** Encapsulation hides *data* behind an interface (how the class protects its state). Abstraction hides *complexity* — exposing what an object does, not how (Day 5).
✍️ **Q: Difference between private and protected?** Protected members are also accessible inside derived classes; private ones are not.
✍️ **Q: Is a class with public data members encapsulated?** No — anyone can put the object into an invalid state.
- **Q: What is data hiding?** The mechanism (private members) that achieves encapsulation.
- **Q: Default access in class vs struct?** class → private, struct → public.

micro.title: Hashing — remember what you have seen

sections.title: Micro-theory (10 minutes)
sections.body:
Yesterday you kept a few variables about the past. Today you keep **everything** about the past — in a hash map — so any question "have I seen X?" costs O(1).

✍️ A hash table computes where a key lives instead of searching for it, so insert and lookup are O(1) on average ([[hash-table-internals#picture]]).
✍️ `unordered_map<key, value>`: `mp[k]++` to count, `mp.count(k)` / `mp.find(k)` to ask. **`mp[k]` inserts a missing key** — never use it just to ask ([[cpp-unordered-map-set#bracket-trap]]).
✍️ Small dense keys (letters) → a plain array `int cnt[26]` beats any map ([[cpp-container-choice#rule]]).

Two patterns today:
- **Complement lookup** — for each x, ask whether its partner (target − x) has already appeared ([[hash-complement-lookup#idea]]).
- **Frequency counting** — count once, answer every "how many" in O(1) ([[hash-frequency-counting#idea]]).

sections.title: Pattern card
sections.body:
✍️ COMPLEMENT LOOKUP — trigger: "pair that sums/differs to …", unsorted. need = target − x; check map; THEN insert x.
✍️ FREQUENCY COUNT — trigger: "anagram, same characters, appears more than, most frequent, duplicate". One table, ++ for one input, −− for the other.
✍️ START OF RUN — trigger: "longest consecutive", O(n), unsorted. Only walk from v where v−1 is missing.
